keep: He owned no country's flag, so he flew whichever one the rule did not reach; in 1954 three of the rules reached back at once.
lede: He left Smyrna a refugee in 1922. By 1954 the United States Justice Department, the Peruvian navy and Aramco were all moving against him, in the same year, for the same habit.
copy: He was born in Smyrna, the son of a tobacco merchant, in 1904 by his historian Gelina Harlaftis's reckoning and 1906 by the date the press printed in his lifetime. When the Turkish army took the city in 1922 the family fled to Greece. Time's 1968 version sends him to Argentina at seventeen with sixty dollars in his pocket. Harlaftis's version is less romantic: a boy raised in a bourgeois milieu who made capital in the Argentine tobacco trade and moved it into shipping in the early 1930s. The first ships are told the same way. Time has six Canadian National vessels bought in 1930 at $20,000 apiece. Harlaftis has two, named after his parents, at £3,750 each. In 1938 Götaverken in Sweden launched Ariston, the first of three tankers he had built there.

The habit was using whichever flag the rule did not reach. After the war he bought American surplus ships through American companies, which the law required to be controlled by American citizens. The government said his were controlled by him, and a grand jury sat from September 1952. In January 1954 he signed an agreement with Saudi Arabia for a national tanker company with first call on the kingdom's oil. The State Department went to work on it, and by December the king was pleased with an arbitration that would let him, in the ambassador's report, "finish with Onassis". The tribunal found for Aramco in 1958. The American case closed in December 1955. The popular account, repeated by Harlaftis in 2012, is that he pleaded guilty and paid a $7 million fine. The Washington Post's report of the settlement says otherwise. The $7 million was a civil settlement. Six of his corporations pleaded guilty and were fined $160,000 between them, and the charges against him were dropped at the government's request.

The whaling is the part with no settlement in it. From 1950 to 1956 his factory ship Olympic Challenger sailed with a German crew under the flags of Panama and Honduras; Panama did not ratify the whaling convention until 1953. The Norwegian whaling association accused it in 1955 of hunting out of season, inside the sanctuaries, and below the minimum size. In November 1954 the Peruvian navy seized the factory ship and several of its catchers inside Peru's 200-mile zone. They were released after 27 days for $3 million, which Lloyd's paid under his policy against seizure. In the spring of 1956 he sold the fleet to Japan for 35.7 million marks. The historian Klaus Barthelmess counts some 22,000 whales in five seasons, a large share of them taken in breach of the convention.

facts.s: His birth year: 1904 in Gelina Harlaftis, 'Creating Global Shipping' (Cambridge University Press, 2019), introduction; 20 January 1906 in 'From Camelot to Elysium (Via Olympic Airways)', Time, 25 October 1968, the date printed in his lifetime. Harlaftis's 2012 draft paper gave 1900. No birth record has been opened here

The price of each of his first two ships, bought from Canadian National Steamships: Gelina Harlaftis, 'Confronting the Russian and United States governments', Bocconi lecture paper, March 2012, resting on Foustanos, 'Onassis: Pioneering in Shipping' (Argo, 2006), p. 27. Time, 25 October 1968, as above, has six ships in 1930 at $20,000 apiece
Ariston launched at Götaverken, Gothenburg, the first of three tankers built there by 1942: Harlaftis, Bocconi paper, 2012, as above

The Onassis agreement with the Saudi government, ratified by royal decree on 9 April 1954: the Aramco arbitration award, International Law Reports 27 (1963), as reproduced by trans-lex.org; FRUS 1952–54, vol. IX pt 1, doc. 341. The tribunal's award, for Aramco, is dated 23 August 1958: 'Saudi Arabia v. Arabian American Oil Company', WorldCat record 12379940. The king's 'finish with Onassis': FRUS, same volume, doc. 377, Jidda, 18 December 1954

The civil settlement, the fines on six corporations, and the dismissal of the charges against four individuals including Onassis: 'Onassis Settles With U.S. for $7 Million', Washington Post and Times Herald, 22 December 1955, read in the CIA Reading Room copy (CIA-RDP75-00149R000600090037-0). The charges: United States v. Onassis, 125 F. Supp. 190 (D.D.C. 1954)
The Peruvian seizure of November 1954 and the payment that released the ships, from Lloyd's: Klaus Barthelmess, 'Die Gegner der Olympic Challenger', Polarforschung 79(3), 2009, pp. 155–176

The sale of the whaling fleet to Kyokuyo Hogei Kaisha in the spring of 1956: Barthelmess, as above, citing Der Spiegel 18/1956, p. 23. Time in 1968 called $8.5 million his profit on it; at the price, it looks like the whole sum

Processed in five seasons, 'a major proportion' in contravention of the 1946 convention: Barthelmess, as above, English abstract. The Norwegian accusation: New York Times, 13 October 1955, read in the CIA Reading Room copy (CIA-RDP75-00149R000600090040-6)

Maheu's account and his 'a crock': Washington Post, 2 August 1978, read in the CIA Reading Room copy (CIA-RDP81M00980R002100100037-8). His lawyer Edward J. Ross on the 'completely unfounded' allegations: New York Times, 1954, CIA Reading Room copy (CIA-RDP75-00149R000600090097-4)

bio.why: Written by a Sunday Times team under Fraser's name, and the one his business historian trusts: Gelina Harlaftis calls it 'the most reliable account' and says Peter Evans's 'Ari', the most quoted, is 'of doubtful quality'. For the ships rather than the man, read Harlaftis's 'Creating Global Shipping' (2019), built on archives she had to assemble herself, the FBI's files among them.

contested: The deepest argument is over what the surplus-ship case was. The government's theory was fraud: American companies that were American on paper only. His lawyer called the allegations completely unfounded, and Harlaftis argues the government was never sure it could win on what 'control' meant. The settlement settled neither. The second argument is over who ended his Saudi agreement and his whaling. In 1978 Robert Maheu, a former FBI agent, confirmed that Stavros Niarchos had hired him to undermine the agreement, and told the Washington Post he had cleared it first with the CIA; he called the larger conspiracy in Jim Hougan's Playboy account 'a crock'. Barthelmess finds 'reason to assume' American agents also pushed Peru. The third is over the historian. Harlaftis's recent work was supported by the Onassis Foundation, and Marc Levinson, reviewing it in 2025, warned that it is sympathetic to its subject and not the final word on the Saudi affair.
